   Risk-Controlled Selective LLM Answering by Pricing Label-Free Checks

Dongyub Jude Lee1,∗ jude.lee@zoom.us Jungseob Lee2,∗ omanma1928@korea.ac.kr Chanjun Park3 chanjun.park@ssu.ac.kr Hyeonseok Moon4,† hyns.moon@sookmyung.ac.kr Heuiseok Lim2,† limhseok@korea.ac.kr
1Zoom Communications   2Korea University 3Soongsil University   4Sookmyung Women’s University
Abstract

Serving an answer from a large language model requires deciding when to abstain, yet a verifier’s ranking accuracy alone does not determine the error rate among served answers. We introduce PriceCheck, which builds a compact family of decision rules from label-free checks such as re-solving a problem. Each check has a price: its agreement rates on correct and incorrect answers and its cost per run. Prices fitted on a small, class-enriched labelled set compose into predictions of a schedule’s coverage and cost, guiding which checks to run and when to stop. A calibration test then selects a schedule at a stated selective-risk target. In mathematics, the selected schedules serve 76.1% of answers on average and keep held-out selective risk below 1.5% on all 15 splits. Under the shared testing protocol, PriceCheck serves more answers at that target than reward models, a prompted judge, the generator’s confidence and a trained correctness classifier. At matched coverage, it keeps the fewest wrong answers among these scorers. Across 118 diagnostic schedules, price-based coverage predictions have a rank correlation of 0.97 with observed coverage. These results show that choosing how checks are combined and stopped matters alongside how well a verifier ranks answers. Code is available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/PriceCheck.
$*$$*$footnotetext: Equal contribution.††footnotetext: Corresponding authors.

1 Introduction

Large language models increasingly rely on a verifier to choose among the candidate answers they generate. The verifier may take a majority vote among the candidates (Wang et al., 2022), apply a trained reward model (Cobbe et al., 2021; Uesato et al., 2022; Lightman et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024), or prompt a model to judge the work (Zheng et al., 2023; Weng et al., 2023). The resulting ranking is enough to pick a winner. However, it does not tell a deployed system how often the answers it serves are wrong, a quantity known as selective risk. Selective prediction studies when to abstain so as to control this risk (Geifman and El‐Yaniv, 2017; Kamath et al., 2020), and distribution-free risk control can certify that it stays below a stated target on held-out calibration data (Bates et al., 2021; Angelopoulos et al., 2022; Angelopoulos et al., 2021). Evaluations of verifier rankings (Zhang et al., 2025) therefore leave a further design question: which checks should a system run, combine and stop to serve many answers at a stated risk target?

Connecting ranking to selective answering requires choosing the rules to test. In a finite-family application of Learn-then-Test, candidate rules are fixed independently of calibration data, and the multiplicity correction grows with the number of rules (Angelopoulos et al., 2021). The family should therefore be small and well chosen. Available label-free checks differ both in how often they agree with wrong answers and in what they cost. A ranking alone does not specify which checks to combine, in what order, or when to stop.

Figure 1 summarises PriceCheck, our approach to pricing and scheduling these checks. A check reads a candidate answer, but not its label, and returns a binary verdict on whether it agrees with that answer. Examples include a re-solve that reaches the same answer (Wang et al., 2022) and a backward probe that recovers an answer from reconstructed reasoning (Weng et al., 2023). We attach a price to each check: its completeness, or agreement rate on correct answers; its leak, or agreement rate on wrong answers; and its unit cost. We fit the rates on a labelled pricing set.

A schedule uses one or more checks to serve an answer or abstain; its coverage is the share of answers served. Composing check prices gives estimates of schedule coverage and cost. This includes cascades that pass a cheap check’s undecided cases to a costlier check. We test a declared family on calibration data and select a schedule at a stated selective-risk target (Angelopoulos et al., 2021). Pricing thus connects measurements of individual checks to the choice of a complete answering rule.

We evaluate PriceCheck on answers to competition mathematics problems (Hendrycks et al., 2021) produced by five fine-tuned generators. Under the shared calibration-testing protocol, we compare with process and outcome reward models, a prompted judge, the generator’s confidence (Kadavath et al., 2022), and a classifier trained on the calibration labels. Across 118 diagnostic schedules, price-based coverage predictions have a rank correlation of 0.97 with observed coverage. At the primary 1.5% target, the selected schedules serve 76.1% of answers on average, keep held-out risk below the target on all 15 splits, and retain fewer wrong answers than every rival scorer at matched coverage.

We also examine the dependence among answers to the same problem (Kish, 1965). Counting each served problem once widens the nominal risk bounds while preserving the advantage of the selected re-solve votes over the trained process reward model. Together, these findings connect the choice of check schedules to coverage and observed risk, beyond the ranking quality of a verifier alone.

2 Related Work

Verifiers that order candidates.

Step-level process reward models learn from step annotations and return a score per solution (Uesato et al., 2022; Lightman et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2027), whereas outcome-level models score the finished answer, some of them writing the verdict as text (Cobbe et al., 2021; Dong et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). Prompting a capable model to grade another’s work needs no annotation at all (Zheng et al., 2023; Yamauchi et al., 2026), and the generator’s own confidence in what it wrote is cheaper still (Kadavath et al., 2022; Tian et al., 2023; Kuhn et al., 2023; Manakul et al., 2023; Panov et al., 2026), although models do not reliably notice their own errors (Huang et al., 2023; Stechly et al., 2023; Lee and Park, 2026). An ordering selects a winner but does not name an operating point, and, as our experiments show, it is also a poor guide to what a scorer can certify. We therefore learn no score and instead measure two rates per check, fitted once on a small labelled probe.

Checks and sampling controllers.

Our backward probe descends from checks that re-derive something the answer ought to imply, such as a masked condition (Weng et al., 2023), a masked quantity (Jiang et al., 2024), the premises a chain of thought assumed (Xue et al., 2023), or the specification a program was written from (Allamanis et al., 2024). Related checks read the derivation as written (Ling et al., 2023; Madaan et al., 2023). In parallel, sampling controllers spend a budget rather than pass a verdict, through a fixed vote over sampled solutions (Wang et al., 2022), variants that stop once the vote settles (Aggarwal et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024), and studies of how to allocate the budget (Brown et al., 2024; Snell et al., 2024; Zuo et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026a). However, both return a decision without the rates that would predict how a chain of checks behaves or which check is worth its cost. We split agreement into its rate on correct and on wrong answers, charge a unit cost on three axes, and predict the coverage of a schedule, cascades included, before it runs.

Distribution-free guarantees.

Serving an answer only when a score clears a threshold is selective prediction (Chow, 1970; El‐Yaniv and Wiener, 2010; Geifman and El‐Yaniv, 2017; Kamath et al., 2020), and distribution-free calibration turns such a threshold into a finite-sample statement about a predictive set (Vovk et al., 2005; Angelopoulos and Bates, 2021), a risk functional (Bates et al., 2021; Angelopoulos et al., 2022), or a family of configurations tested at once (Angelopoulos et al., 2021). Applications abstain on a generation or filter the claims inside one (Quach et al., 2023; Yadkori et al., 2024; Nguyen et al., 2026). We build on this machinery rather than replace it. The binomial test assumes independent calibration answers and takes the candidate family as given. PriceCheck uses prices to construct that family and assesses within-problem dependence with problem-count risk bounds.

3 PriceCheck

We first define the price of a check, then how prices compose into schedules, and finally the certificate. Throughout, a candidate answer is one stored pair of a problem and a proposed answer, and an action, our term for a check, returns a single binary observation on a candidate answer, which records whether it agrees with the proposal. No action reads a correctness label when it runs.

Problem formulation.

Let x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} denote a problem, y^∈𝒴\hat{y}\in\mathcal{Y} the proposed answer a generator produces for it, and y∗∈𝒴y^{*}\in\mathcal{Y} the ground-truth answer, so that (x,y^)(x,\hat{y}) is a candidate answer. We write its latent correctness indicator as Y=𝕀⁡(y^=y∗)Y=\mathbb{I}(\hat{y}=y^{*}). A selective rule S⁡(x,y^)∈{0,1}S(x,\hat{y})\in\{0,1\} serves the candidate answer when S=1S=1 and abstains when S=0S=0. Schedules in Section 3.2 build such rules from actions. A rule is evaluated by its coverage C⁡(S)=ℙ⁡(S=1)C(S)=\mathbb{P}(S=1) and its selective risk

R⁡(S)=ℙ⁡(Y=0∣S=1),R(S)\;=\;\mathbb{P}(Y=0\mid S=1), (1)

the error rate among served answers. Given a selective-risk target α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) and a confidence budget δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), our objective is to select and certify a schedule SS for which ℙ⁡(R⁡(S)≤α)≥1−δ\mathbb{P}\bigl(R(S)\leq\alpha\bigr)\geq 1-\delta, where the probability is over the draw of calibration data, at the largest coverage C⁡(S)C(S) we can obtain.

3.1 The price of an action

We define the price of an action as two measured rates and a unit cost. Writing V∈{0,1}V\in\{0,1\} for the verdict of one draw, the completeness p1=ℙ⁡(V=1∣Y=1)p_{1}=\mathbb{P}(V=1\mid Y=1) is the per-draw rate at which the action agrees with a correct answer, and the leak p0=ℙ⁡(V=1∣Y=0)p_{0}=\mathbb{P}(V=1\mid Y=0) is the per-draw rate at which it agrees with a wrong one. The unit cost is the cost of one draw. Table 3.1 lists both rates for our seven actions, together with the unit cost on two of our three cost axes, generated tokens and parameter-weighted tokens. The two axes do not order the actions identically, so we carry both through the analysis.

Backward probe. Given the problem and the proposed answer, a reverse model writes the reasoning that leads to that answer, and a forward model then recovers an answer from that trace (Weng et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2026b). Each draw is one such trace and recovery, and its verdict is whether the recovered answer agrees with the proposed one. We take K=3K=3 draws and record the agreement count m∈{0,…,K}m\in\{0,\dots,K\}. We run the probe at three model sizes, 8B, 4B and 1.7B, and give both prompts verbatim in Appendix A.3.

Re-solve vote. For every distinct problem, we draw fresh solutions from the frozen forward model, 16 at 8B and 8 at 1.7B, and each draw casts a vote whose verdict is whether its answer agrees with the proposed answer (Wang et al., 2022). A draw with no extractable answer counts as disagreement, since a schedule must not serve an answer on a verdict it cannot read.

Generator confidence. Two further actions read the generator’s own confidence: its probability of Yes when asked whether the proposed answer is correct, and the mean log-probability of the stored solution (Kadavath et al., 2022). We set each threshold to maximise completeness minus leak on the full pool, defining a descriptive one-draw action charged one scoring pass with no generated tokens.

Fitting the price. Our prediction experiments fit p1p_{1} and p0p_{0} on a class-enriched pricing set of 100 labelled candidate answers, stratified by generator with at least eight wrong answers. Appendix A.10 gives the sampling recipe and overdispersion estimate; Table 3.1 reports descriptive rates on the full pool.
